column1: # Every SYNTAX-class fixture in compiler/reject_class.tsv, and what the Zed
# tree-sitter grammar does with it.  Three columns: path, verdict, reason.
# scripts/editors_check.sh asserts this table against a real parse: a fixture
# recorded ACCEPTED that starts failing, or one recorded REJECTED that starts
# parsing, reddens the lane by name.  A SYNTAX fixture missing from this table
# also reddens, so a new one cannot join the accepted blob unclassified.
# ACCEPTED is not a defect report.  grammar.js is a highlighting grammar: it has
# no external scanner, so it is whitespace-insensitive, and it does no name
# resolution, no arity counting and no value-range checking.  Each row says
# which of those the fixture needs.

column3: `1 = 2` is an assignment whose left side is an expression; which expressions are PLACES is a rule the flat grammar does not carry
an expression is a legal statement in grammar.js; "has no effect" is a check on the expression's KIND, not on its shape
`bounded["x"]int` is grammatical -- the capacity slot takes any expression, and "an integer literal or an int const" is a value check
the char rule needs one character between the quotes, so `''` leaves it unmatched
the char rule takes any backslash byte; the escape ALPHABET is checked in tychoc's lexer
the char rule spells exactly one character, so `'ab'` leaves the literal unterminated
'?' is in no token rule, so the grammar has nothing to match it with
`//` lexes as two division operators; refusing it is tychoc's lexer telling a C programmer what went wrong
same as assign_to_literal for `+=` -- the place rule is tychoc's, not the grammar's
needs the const initialiser EVALUATED; the division parses
needs the const initialiser EVALUATED; the division parses
needs "a const initialiser is one scalar literal"; the grammar admits any expression there
same rule as const_expr_float, reached through an identifier
same rule as const_expr_float, reached through a call
same as const_div_overflow, reached through a shift
`delete f()["a"]` parses; "the map must be a place" is a rule on the KIND of the receiver
`delete m` parses as a delete of an expression; requiring an index is tychoc's
a ceiling (8 destructuring targets); the grammar repeats without counting
`0..<N` is grammatical everywhere; restricting it to a `parallel for` head is a context rule
two fields named `x` parse; duplicate detection needs a symbol table
a ceiling (16 type parameters); the grammar repeats without counting
`Err()` is a well-formed call; the refusal is about the Result's error type
a qualified name is a legal array length in the grammar; "must be known at parse time" is a resolution rule
a value-range check on a literal that lexes correctly
`1e` lexes as INT then IDENT in both, and with no newline rule the grammar takes the IDENT as its own expression
`1e400` is a well-formed float token; out-of-range is a value check
a ceiling (8 parameters in a function type)
the grammar makes the three-clause `for` init optional; tychoc requires it
every token is well-formed; the flat grammar has no `for` head that could require a condition clause
as above for the post clause -- a missing clause is an arity rule on a head this grammar does not build
`;` is an ordinary operator token here; "exactly three clauses" counts them, which the flat grammar does not
a call is a legal statement, so the init clause parses; "a declaration or an assignment" counts kinds
as above for the post clause
a three-clause `for` with only two clauses; counting the ';' separators is tychoc's
`:=` and `:` are both ordinary operator tokens; which one may end a `for` head is a rule with no head to apply to
`for k, v in xs:` parses; "a for binds one name" is an arity rule on the binder list
the string rule takes any backslash byte; the escape ALPHABET is checked in tychoc's lexer
`close: h_free` is a well-formed body line; that the keyword must be `free` is a spelling rule inside the handle body
same string rule as fstring_escape -- \x is consumed, not validated
the grammar spells \x with exactly two hex digits, so a one-digit escape leaves the string unterminated
an `if` with no `else` is grammatical; requiring one in VALUE position needs to know the position
grammar.js has no external scanner, so it is whitespace-insensitive and cannot see an indent level at all
`0b2` lexes as `0` then `b2`, and with no newline rule the trailing identifier is its own expression
`0x` lexes as `0` then `x`, same as int_bin_bad_digit
a well-formed hex token whose VALUE exceeds int64
a well-formed decimal token whose VALUE exceeds int64
`a is X is Y` chains a binary operator, which the grammar allows; forbidding the chain is tychoc's
the grammar's identifier rule does not exclude reserved words in field position
same identifier rule, in binding position
`map_del(...)` is an ordinary call; the removal is enforced by name resolution
as map_del_removed
as map_del_removed
as map_del_removed
`[string: int]` parses as an index expression; telling type from value needs the context
which scalars may follow '-' in an arm is a value rule, not a shape
a string in a `|` set parses as a literal; which literals a scalar arm takes is tychoc's
`2.."z"` parses -- the range rule takes expressions on both sides, and which literals may be a match arm is tychoc's
`a..b` parses whatever the two ends are; "same kind of value" is a type check
grammar.js has no external scanner and emits no INDENT/DEDENT, so indentation cannot be wrong
`packed struct` has no rule in grammar.js -- `packed` parses as an ordinary identifier and the field-type rule needs the symbol table anyway
`packed` before a non-struct declaration is refused by parse_struct; the flat grammar has no `packed` rule and reads the word as an identifier
`1..<4` is grammatical everywhere; requiring a literal `0` in a `parallel for` head is a value check
`parallel` then a declaration parses as two statements; that `parallel` must be followed by `for` is a context rule
`range(N)` is an ordinary call; the removal is enforced by name resolution
the raw-string rule needs a closing backtick, and there is none
`bogus:` is a well-formed arm head; the three legal spellings are checked by name in tychoc
no newline rule, so a trailing `;` ends nothing and the statement still parses
`spawn x` parses; requiring the operand to be a CALL is a rule on its kind
as fstring_escape -- the escape alphabet is not the grammar's
the string rule takes any byte that is not a quote; refusing a raw control byte is tychoc's lexer
the string rule needs a closing quote
a ceiling (16 type parameters)
`yield &<expr>` parses; "rooted in a parameter" is a dataflow rule
a `return` is a legal body; "a single `yield &<place>`" is a rule on what the body CONTAINS
`-> int` is a well-formed return type; requiring `inout` there is tychoc's
`yield <expr>` parses; place-ness is not a syntactic property here
counting uses of a parameter inside the yielded place needs name resolution
no external scanner, so tabs and spaces are both just whitespace
as tab_mix

a one-element parenthesised type parses as a grouping; the minimum is an arity rule
no newline rule, so two statements on one line are two statements
`id$()` parses as an empty type-argument list; requiring at least one is an arity rule
`where Q: ...` parses; whether `Q` is a type parameter needs the signature's scope
the grammar's identifier rule has no case classes, so `Ok` binds like any name
as upper_bind_local_used, in parameter position
a match arm ending in a statement parses; "must end in a value" needs the arm's position
`inout ...int` is a well-formed parameter; that the two modifiers exclude each other is tychoc's
the parameter list parses in any order; "last" is a positional rule tychoc enforces
a ceiling (8 payload fields)
as typeset_badtp -- the name resolves, or does not, outside the grammar
a ceiling (8 constraints)
a `where` clause parses on any signature; requiring a `$T` is a signature rule
